samples.summary: Production entrypoint uses `program.parse()` (sync) with async action handlers, so the behavior the new `--quiet` guard asserts via `parseAsync` is not what ships
samples.evidence: `bin.ts:27` calls `program.parse()`, but every registered action is `async function (...)` (e.g. `docs.ts:70`, `cells.ts:16`). Commander only awaits action promises in `parseAsync`; with `parse()` the returned promise is dropped. The new regression guard (`test/output.test.ts:240`) drives `parseAsync`, so it proves the body/error-envelope behavior only for a path the binary never takes. Any action rejection becomes an unhandled rejection (raw Node stack, no `{error:{code,message}}` envelope, exit code not the one `outputError` set), and nothing keeps the process alive until the async action completes. `parseAsync().catch(outputError)` would make the guard faithful.

samples.summary: `sheets cells batch` parses JSON outside its try/catch, so malformed input escapes the error-envelope path entirely
samples.evidence: `cells.ts:110-120` runs `JSON.parse(dataStr)` and the stdin read/`JSON.parse` before the `try` that starts at line 132. A bad `--data '{'` (or a stdin read error) throws inside the async action, bypassing `outputError`, so no `{error:{code:'ERROR',message:...}}` reaches stderr and `process.exitCode = 1` is never set. Combined with `bin.ts:27`'s `program.parse()` (no `parseAsync`, no `.catch`), it surfaces as an unhandled-rejection trace — exactly the invariant the delta's new test ('prints the error envelope on stderr and exits 1') claims to protect, on a command the guard does not cover.
searchedFor: read cells.ts, sheets-import.ts, docs.ts action bodies for code outside try

samples.summary: `sheets export` emits its progress notice on stdout (console.log), not stderr, violating the stdout=body-only rule this PR codifies
samples.evidence: `sheets-export.ts:52-54` does `if (!opts.quiet) console.log(`Exported to ${file}`)`. Every other notice goes to stderr (`binary.ts:59`, `docs/content.ts:142`, `docs.ts:292`). Since `formatter.ts:18-28` now documents stdout as 'the data callers redirect', this notice on stdout means `wafflebase sheets export doc out.csv | jq` receives a non-JSON line. samples.summary: New tests drive commander without `exitOverride()`, so any parse error would `process.exit()` and tear down the vitest worker instead of failing one test
samples.evidence: `run()` at `test/output.test.ts:238-241` calls `buildProgram().parseAsync(...)` on a program from `createProgram()` (`root.ts:42`), which never calls `.exitOverride()`. If flag resolution ever changes (a subcommand redeclares `--quiet`, or `enablePositionalOptions()` is adopted so trailing program options become unknown), commander's error path calls `process.exit(1)`, aborting the whole test file rather than failing one assertion — masking the regression the guard exists to catch.

finding.summary: Production entrypoint uses `program.parse()` (sync) with async action handlers, so the behavior the new `--quiet` guard asserts via `parseAsync` is not what ships
finding.evidence: `bin.ts:27` calls `program.parse()`, but every registered action is `async function (...)` (e.g. `docs.ts:70`, `cells.ts:16`). Commander only awaits action promises in `parseAsync`; with `parse()` the returned promise is dropped. The new regression guard (`test/output.test.ts:240`) drives `parseAsync`, so it proves the body/error-envelope behavior only for a path the binary never takes. Any action rejection becomes an unhandled rejection (raw Node stack, no `{error:{code,message}}` envelope, exit code not the one `outputError` set), and nothing keeps the process alive until the async action completes. `parseAsync().catch(outputError)` would make the guard faithful.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo: bin.ts:27 is literally `program.parse();` (sole entrypoint, no trailing await/catch), while essentially every registered action is `async function` (docs.ts:70/145/174/230, cells.ts:16/37, login.ts:16; 35 `.action(` sites total) under commander ^13 (package.json:26), which only chains action promises in `parseAsync`. So the action promise is dropped in production. The new --quiet regression guard exercises the other path (`await buildProgram().parseAsync(...)` at test/output.test.ts:240; the only other parseAsync use is scripts/debug-cmd.mjs:15), so it does not cover the shipped path. The consequence is concretely reachable: commands/login.ts:16-140 has no try/catch at all, and its rejections (startCallbackServer reject at login.ts:246/266, 30s timeout reject at login.ts:232, bare fetch at login.ts:56/75/92, decodeJwtExpiry throws at session.ts:99/109) become unhandled rejections instead of the `{error:{code,message}}` envelope produced by output/formatter.ts:52-58; other commands also do pre-try work outside their guard (docs.ts:146-150, cells.ts:43-55). No guard or wrapper anywhere makes this unreachable, and the issue is in-lane (dropped await / unhandled rejection / mis-handled failure). The reviewer's secondary claim about the process not staying alive is weaker (pending libuv I/O usually keeps the loop alive), but that does not refute the dropped-promise error-handling defect.

Combined with `bin.ts:27`'s `program.parse()` (no `parseAsync`, no `.catch`), it surfaces as an unhandled-rejection trace — exactly the invariant the delta's new test ('prints the error envelope on stderr and exits 1') claims to protect, on a command the guard does not cover.

verdict.reason: The described code is present exactly as claimed. In `cells.ts` the `batch` action parses `--data` JSON at line 112 and reads/parses stdin at lines 116-119, all before the `try` that starts at line 132 and only wraps the HTTP call. `outputError` (formatter.ts:52-58) is the sole emitter of the `{error:{code,message}}` envelope and the sole setter of `process.exitCode = 1`, and it is reachable only from the `catch` at cells.ts:140. `bin.ts:27` calls `program.parse()` (not `parseAsync`) with no `.catch`, and `root.ts:42-63` installs no `unhandledRejection`/`uncaughtException` handler or `exitOverride`; a grep across packages/cli finds those only in a test helper and a debug script. Therefore a malformed `--data '{'` or a stdin read error rejects the async action handler, commander drops it, and the CLI emits an unhandled-rejection trace instead of the error envelope. Sibling subcommands (get/set/delete) keep their fallible work inside `try`, showing the asymmetry is unintentional. Real, reachable, and in the correctness lane (mis-handled failure bypassing the error path).
